evidence.note: Opened with a distinct environment/understanding stage (workspace, data format, tokenizer, GPU/PyTorch, package availability) before writing any training code — a deliberate first milestone.

Before the first long run, ran concrete pre-launch gates: syntax check, model creation, save/load round-trip, cross_entropy-contract check (step 10), and compressed checkpoint size vs 32MB. Repeatedly resized (54M→32.5M→30M) until compressed size fit under budget — an explicit size-budget done-check preceding training.

The size gate was NOT robustly front-loaded: the agent repeatedly LAUNCHED long training then killed runs upon discovering the checkpoint grew past 32MB during training (trained weights compress worse than init). Size overflow was rediscovered mid-run several times, wasting compute — the high-risk invalidator was not retired before the expensive step.

torch.compile C-compiler crash and the val_bpb metric miscalculation were both discovered at runtime rather than caught by a cheap pre-flight check, indicating reactive rather than fully risk-ordered gating.

Later milestone-driven adaptation: introduced raw-binary format and lzma to reclaim space, then sized a 19-layer/29.3M model with an explicit ~6.75MB margin (25.2MB init) so the size gate would survive training growth — a concrete, quantitative gate finally set before the final run.

reasoning: The agent clearly staged the work: understand environment → write script → verify param count/compressed size/save-load/cross_entropy contract → launch → measure local val_bpb → scale/resize, with concrete pre-launch success criteria (fits 32MB with margin, round-trip loads, contract holds). That is more than anchor 5's rough criteria, matching the concrete-gate spirit of anchor 8. But it falls short of 8/10 because the ordering was not risk-optimal: the size-overflow failure mode was rediscovered deep inside multiple expensive runs rather than retired up front, and crashes/metric bugs surfaced at runtime — so the milestones read as an implicit, partly-reactive sequence rather than a front-loaded, quantitatively-gated hierarchy. This lands at 6.
